title: Fishermen and Gates
statement:
A lake has `N` fishing spots in a row, numbered `1` to `N`. Neighbouring spots are `1` metre apart. There are exactly **3 gates**. Gate `i` stands at the position of spot `p_i` and has `f_i` fishermen waiting to enter. The distance from a gate to the spot at its own position is also `1` metre, so a fisherman who ends up at spot `s` of gate `p` walks `|p - s| + 1` metres. For example, with a gate at position `4`, a fisherman who takes spot `4` walks `1` m, one who takes spot `3` or `5` walks `2` m, and so on.

The gates are opened **one at a time**, in an order you choose, and **all fishermen of a gate must have taken their spots before the next gate is opened**. Inside a gate, the fishermen enter one after another, and each of them takes the **nearest free spot** (a spot not yet taken by anyone, including fishermen from earlier gates).

Sometimes two free spots are equally near (one on each side of the gate). Then the fisherman may take either of them. Only the **last** fisherman of a gate can actually change the total this way, because every earlier fisherman in a tie leaves the other equally near spot for the next one; so for the last fisherman of each gate you should pick the spot that gives the smallest total walking distance for everybody.

Over all possible orders of opening the gates and all allowed tie choices, find the **minimum possible sum of walking distances** of all fishermen. It is guaranteed that the total number of fishermen does not exceed `N`, so everybody finds a spot.

The input contains several independent test cases; answer each one.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `T`, the number of test cases.
Each test case has `4` lines: the first contains `N`; each of the next three lines contains two integers `p` and `f`, the position of a gate and the number of fishermen waiting at it.
outputFormat: For each test case print one line with the minimum possible total walking distance.
constraints: 1 ≤ p ≤ N, and the three gate positions are distinct
f ≥ 1 for every gate, and the three values of f sum to at most N

examples.explanation: Five independent test cases. In the first one, for instance, N = 10 and gates at 4, 6 and 10 hold 5, 2 and 2 fishermen. Trying all 6 gate orders and the tie choices of each last fisherman gives a best total of 18.

Gate 2 takes spot 2 (1 m) and then spot 1 or 3 (2 m); choosing spot 1 leaves spot 3 for the gate at 3 (1 m). The gate at 5 takes spot 5 (1 m). The total is 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5; choosing spot 3 for the last fisherman of gate 2 would push gate 3 to spot 4 and cost 6.

hints: There are only 3! = 6 orders in which the gates can be opened, so you can simulate every order.
Simulate a gate by repeatedly taking the nearest free spot: check position p - d and p + d for d = 0, 1, 2, ... until one of them is free. The walking distance is d + 1.
A tie only matters for the last fisherman of a gate, so branch into both choices only there (at most 2 branches per gate), and take the minimum total over all orders and branches.
